title: Captioned Phones vs. Amplified Phones: Which Helps With Hearing Loss, and What They Cost
subtitle: A plain-English guide to phones that show callers' words on a screen, phones that simply make voices louder, and how to tell which one fits.
excerpt: If phone calls have turned into a guessing game, a captioned phone or an amplified phone may help. Here is how each works, who qualifies for captioning, and why the phone itself may still cost money even when the captioning service has no monthly fee.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Phone calls are often the first place hearing loss shows up. In person, you can watch someone's face. On the phone, the voice is all you get, and if it sounds muffled, you end up nodding along, asking people to repeat themselves, or letting calls go to voicemail.

There are two common fixes for a home phone. One makes the caller's voice louder. The other shows the caller's words as text on a screen, a bit like subtitles on TV. Which one makes sense depends mostly on how much trouble you have hearing on the phone.

Amplified phones raise the volume of the caller's voice, according to HearingTracker, and are mostly bought privately rather than through a registration program. The Clarity C200 below is one example: it boosts incoming sound, has a loud ringer and a bright visual ring indicator, and has no monthly fee. It is recommended for mild to moderate hearing loss. If your loss is more severe, or you are not sure, an audiologist or doctor can help you decide whether volume alone will be enough.

A captioned phone lets you listen and read at the same time. According to the FCC, the captions travel over the internet, and voice recognition puts the words on screen almost as they are spoken. The FCC calls this IP CTS, short for Internet Protocol Captioned Telephone Service. The FCC describes it as for a person who can speak but has trouble hearing on the phone.
HearingTracker, a hearing-health information site, says the service is funded by the TRS Fund, so eligible users generally do not pay a monthly captioning fee. It puts it this way:
"the captioning service is generally provided at no monthly captioning fee." (HearingTracker)

Two catches. First, free captioning does not always mean a free phone; the equipment can still cost money. Second, you have to qualify. Eligibility is based on hearing loss that makes captions necessary for phone calls, not on age. You register with a provider and certify your hearing loss. Sometimes you can certify it yourself, but an audiologist, hearing aid specialist or doctor may also certify. Federal rules do not allow people without qualifying hearing loss to use the captions.

items: Your connection at home: the captioned phone below needs both a phone line and high-speed internet. A home with only cell phones will not work with it. HearingTracker notes some other captioned phones do not need a landline, so ask about those if that is your situation.
The real cost: check the equipment price, any warranty, and whether long-distance or other charges may apply, even when captioning has no cost.
How loud it gets: volume boost is measured in decibels (dB), a unit of loudness. A higher number means more boost.
Screen and buttons: look for a large screen, adjustable caption text size, and a big, lit keypad if eyesight is also a concern.
Hearing aid compatibility: helpful if the person wears hearing aids.
Returns and warranty: a money-back window lets you see if it truly helps.
Setup help: some makers offer free installation help by phone or in person.
Stock: one retailer lists the C200 as discontinued, so confirm availability before you order.

sections.content: For a captioned phone, start with registration. The provider will ask for certification of hearing loss. If self-certification is not accepted, a quick call to the person's audiologist or doctor can get the form signed. If you are unsure how much hearing loss is involved, that same professional is the right person to ask.

Next, check the spot where the phone will sit. The Hamilton 2400i needs a phone jack and a way to reach the internet, either Wi-Fi or an Ethernet cable. Hamilton offers free installation support by phone or in person, so it is worth using rather than wrestling with settings alone. This guide did not cover Hamilton's app or other providers' monthly plans, and other captioned phone options exist.
Once it is running, keep the same home phone number and make sure caller ID displays correctly. Adjust the caption size and color until reading feels easy.
For the amplified phone, setup is simpler: plug it into the phone jack and mount it on the wall if that works better. Because it is corded, check the spot where it will sit.

Captions are a live or automated transcript, so they can lag behind the speaker or miss words. Use them as a helper, not a perfect record. A captioned phone is also not a cell phone and does not work without internet. Federal rules limit use to registered users, so do not give the phone to someone else to use on their account. As general advice, in an emergency call 911.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: If phone calls have become tiring, it is worth looking into one of these. A little volume may be all someone needs, or seeing the words may make calls feel easier. Either way, a few minutes of setup can help bring back everyday conversations.

products.name: Hamilton CapTel 2400i Captioned Telephone
products.price: $75 to buy outright, including shipping (as shown on Hamilton's page; check current price); captioning service stated as no cost
products.blurb: For people who need to read along on calls: a large touch screen shows captions, with up to 40 dB of volume boost, adjustable text size, and an answering machine that captions messages. Needs a phone line and high-speed internet; comes with a 5-year replacement warranty and 30-day money-back guarantee. Hamilton says equipment charges and standard long-distance charges may apply.

products.name: Clarity C200 Amplified Trimline Phone
products.price: $49.95 at Hear Central (check current price; other retailers list it between about $39 and $70, so check at checkout); no monthly fee
products.blurb: A simple corded phone for mild to moderate hearing loss, boosting voices up to 26 dB with a loud ringer, bright visual ring indicator and large backlit keypad. It shows no captions, and one retailer lists it as discontinued, so confirm stock before ordering.
